name: Timbuktu
info: Timbuktu is a city in Mali, 20 kilometres north of the Niger River, which began as a seasonal Tuareg camp about 1100 CE and became a trading and Islamic scholarly centre under the Mali and Songhai empires.

facts.founded: According to al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan, a seasonal camp of the Maghsharan Tuareg about 1100 CE, which became a permanent town in the 13th or early 14th century; modern scholars hold that the evidence cannot fix the time or the founders.
facts.where: 20 kilometres north of the Niger River, at the southern edge of the Sahara, in the Tombouctou Region of Mali.
facts.known: The trans-Saharan trade in salt and gold; the Djinguereber, Sankoré and Sidi Yahya mosques; its scholars and manuscripts; Mansa Musa and Askia Mohammad I; the Moroccan conquest of 1591; the accounts of Leo Africanus and René Caillié
facts.today: Timbuktu is the capital of Mali's Tombouctou Region, with about eighty thousand people.

t: Timbuktu began as a seasonal Tuareg camp near the Niger, and it grew into a trading town and a centre of Islamic learning as part of the Mali Empire from 1324 and then of the Songhai Empire from 1468 or 1469.

A Moroccan army captured the city on 30 May 1591, scholars were arrested, killed or exiled, and Timbuktu lost its standing as trade moved to Atlantic routes and its rulers changed many times until the French took it in 1893.
Its mosques are World Heritage monuments and its libraries hold manuscripts counted in the hundreds of thousands, which were threatened when armed groups held the city in 2012 and 2013.
dyk: During the occupation of the city by armed groups the librarian Abdel Kader Haidara had metal footlockers, each holding up to 300 manuscripts, distributed to nearly 2,500 safe houses in the city, and about 90% of the manuscripts were saved.
ev: The Tarikh al-Sudan dates the start of the seasonal Tuareg camp to the end of the fifth century of the hijra
Mansa Musa annexes Timbuktu to the Mali Empire on his return from pilgrimage to Mecca
Ibn Battuta visits Timbuktu and Kabara and meets the governor, Farba Musa
The Songhai Empire absorbs Timbuktu, in 1468 or 1469
A Moroccan army captures Timbuktu after the Battle of Tondibi
René Caillié reaches Timbuktu and returns to France to claim the Société de Géographie's prize
French soldiers under Lieutenant Gaston Boiteux annex the city
Tuareg rebels and Islamist groups take Timbuktu, and shrines are destroyed

sections.origins:
Iron Age settlements have been found near Timbuktu, older than the town's traditional foundation date. Thick layers of sand prevent excavation in the town itself, but an Iron Age tell complex 9 kilometres south-east of it was excavated between 2008 and 2010 by archaeologists from Yale University and the Mission Culturelle de Tombouctou. It was first occupied in the 5th century BCE, thrived through the second half of the 1st millennium CE and collapsed in the late 10th or early 11th century. Research as late as 2000 found no remains of the 11th or 12th century within the modern city.

When Abd al-Sadi wrote the Tarikh al-Sudan in the 17th century, from oral tradition, he dated the foundation of Timbuktu as a seasonal camp to the end of the fifth century of the hijra, around 1100 CE. He saw the Maghsharan Tuareg as the founders, whose summer encampment grew from a temporary settlement into a depot and a meeting place for travellers, and became a permanent town in the 13th or early 14th century. By another reckoning the settlement became permanent early in the 12th century, and Leo Africanus wrote that Mansa Sulayman founded the town in 1213 or 1214. Modern scholars say there is not enough evidence to fix the time or the founders.

The town grew from trade between the Middle Niger Delta and the pastoralists of the Sahara, in an area already part of an exchange network with Djenné-Djenno, Dia and the Méma region by the middle of the 1st millennium CE. The river's importance led to the description of Timbuktu as 'a gift of the Niger'.
sections.growth:
The wealth of Timbuktu rested on trade across the Sahara. After a shift in routes in the later 14th century the town flourished on the trade in salt, gold, ivory and slaves from towns and states including Begho of Bonoman and Sijilmassa. In the 14th century it developed as a commercial and religious centre while Walata, the earlier hub of the trans-Saharan trade, declined, and scholars from Walata settled there. In 1375 Timbuktu appeared on the Catalan Atlas, which shows that it was by then a commercial centre linked to North Africa and known to Europe.

Under Askia Mohammad I, who ruled from 1493 to 1528, the city enjoyed a golden age, with a central and regional administration that left its commercial centres room to flourish. Merchants from Ghadames, Awjilah and many other North African cities gathered there to buy gold and slaves in exchange for salt from Taghaza and North African cloth and horses. Its population grew from about 10,000 by 1300 to about 50,000 in the 1500s, and some estimates put its medieval peak at 100,000.

Leo Africanus, who visited in 1512, described abundant grain, cattle, milk and butter, houses of chalk with thatched roofs and scarce salt, which was carried from Taghaza, about 500 miles away, and which he saw sell at eighty ducats a load. He also described a king with many plates and sceptres of gold and learned men maintained at his cost. Until the second half of the 20th century salt from Taoudenni, 664 kilometres north, came by caravans of several thousand camels, which took three weeks each way.
sections.rulers:
Timbuktu began as a Tuareg settlement and was annexed peacefully by Mansa Musa in 1324 on his return from the pilgrimage to Mecca, so becoming part of the Mali Empire. He ordered a royal palace built there. When Ibn Battuta visited in 1353 the governor was Farba Musa, and most inhabitants were Massufa Berbers. In the first half of the 15th century, as Mali weakened, the town became relatively autonomous under Tuareg influence and a leader called Akil Akamalwa.

The Songhai Empire absorbed Timbuktu in 1468 or 1469. It was led in turn by Sunni Ali Ber (1468–1492), Sunni Baru (1492–1493) and Askia Mohammad I (1493–1528), and the Askia dynasty held power until 1591. Sunni Ali Ber was in severe conflict with the city after its conquest.

On 30 May 1591, after the Battle of Tondibi, an expedition of mercenaries called the Arma, sent by the Saadi ruler of Morocco, Ahmad I al-Mansur, and led by the Spanish Muslim Judar Pasha, captured the city in search of gold mines. The Arma became a ruling class and after 1612 were virtually independent of Morocco. Later the Tuareg took control in 1737, Bambara and Kounta occupied or besieged the city, the Massina Empire held it from 1826 until 1865, and then the Toucouleur Empire. The sources conflict on who held it when the French came. On 15 December 1893 a small group of French soldiers under Lieutenant Gaston Boiteux annexed it, and it became part of French Sudan until the Republic of Mali was proclaimed on 22 September 1960.
sections.life:
Timbuktu was a world centre of Islamic learning from the 13th to the 17th century, especially under the Mali Empire and Askia Mohammad I. Mansa Musa recruited scholars from across the Islamic world, who studied not only Islamic subjects but history, rhetoric, law, science and above all medicine. Literacy and books were symbols of wealth, power and blessing, and the acquisition of books became a main concern of scholars. A lively book trade with other parts of the Islamic world and the emperor's support led to thousands of manuscripts.

Teaching went on in informal madrasahs, three of which, Djinguereber, Sidi Yahya and Sankoré, are now called the University of Timbuktu and are said to have served 25,000 students. Education was supported by families or lineages, among them the Aqit and Bunu al-Qadi al-Hajj families. Ahmad Baba al Massufi is regarded as the city's greatest scholar. The three mosques are the city's chief monuments. The Djinguereber Mosque was built in 1327 under Mansa Musa, and the Tarikh al-Sudan and the Tarikh al-fattash attribute it to him. Qadi al-Aqib had it pulled down in 1570 and rebuilt larger. Sankoré was built in the 14th and 15th centuries, and its libraries housed thousands of manuscripts. The Sidi Yahya Mosque was founded in 1400 and completed in 1440.

The earliest surviving local documents are the 17th-century chronicles of al-Sadi, the Tarikh al-Sudan, and of Ibn al-Mukhtar, the Tarikh al-fattash. They record the biographies of imams and judges and say little of the town's social and economic history.
sections.crises:
When the Songhai Empire absorbed Timbuktu in 1468 and 1469, many scholars left for Walata. In 1591 the Moroccan conquest began a period of economic and intellectual decline, and in 1593 Ahmad I al-Mansur, citing disloyalty, had many of the city's scholars arrested and then killed or exiled, among them Ahmad Baba, who was forced to move to Marrakesh and returned, dying in Timbuktu in 1627. Trans-Atlantic trade, which carried enslaved Africans including leaders and scholars of Timbuktu, pushed the city aside as a trade and learning centre.

Droughts in 1973 and 1985 reduced the Tuareg herders round Timbuktu, and many people left for Algeria and Libya. After a military coup in Bamako on 21 March 2012, the Tuareg MNLA and Ansar Dine took Timbuktu on 1 April. On 3 April Ansar Dine announced that its version of sharia would be enforced, and the mayor said almost all of the city's Christians then fled. The MNLA declared the independence of Azawad on 6 April, but Ansar Dine and AQMI installed sharia. In May and June 2012 Ansar Dine destroyed shrines, including the mausoleum of Sidi Mahmoud, with shovels and pickaxes, calling them idolatry.

On 25 January 2013 fifteen men entered the restoration rooms of the Ahmed Baba Institute and burned 4,202 manuscripts. Most manuscripts survived, because families had hidden them and the librarian Abdel Kader Haidara organised their removal; some 350,000 were taken to safety, and most of them stayed in Bamako for years. French and Malian soldiers retook the city on 28 January 2013. On 8 August 2023 the armed group JNIM blockaded Timbuktu.
sections.legacy:
Leo Africanus, born in Granada in 1485, wrote an account of the city in his Descrittione dell'Africa, published in 1550. In 1780 the Moroccan Shabeni described a very different Timbuktu. These accounts made the city's reputation in Europe shift from rich to mysterious. In 1788 the African Association was founded in England to find it, and the Société de Géographie in Paris offered a prize of 9,000 francs in 1824 to the first non-Muslim to reach the town and return with information. Gordon Laing arrived in August 1826 and was killed the next month by local Muslims who feared European intervention. René Caillié arrived in 1828, disguised as a Muslim, and returned to claim the prize. Heinrich Barth reached the city in 1853, and Oskar Lenz and Cristobal Benítez in 1880. The African Association's first explorer, Mungo Park, set out for the Niger and Timbuktu in 1795 and 1805 and died in modern-day Nigeria without reporting his findings. The claim of the American sailor Robert Adams to have been there in 1812 is doubted.

In 1988 three mosques and 16 mausoleums or cemeteries of the old town were inscribed on the World Heritage list. The site was on the List in Danger from 1990 to 2005 and again from 2012.

Libraries in Timbuktu are said to have held up to 700,000 manuscripts. Timbuktu is now the capital of Mali's Tombouctou Region, with about eighty thousand people, fewer than at its medieval peak of an estimated 100,000.

summary: Timbuktu grew from a seasonal Tuareg camp near the Niger into a trading town and a centre of Islamic learning under the Mali and Songhai empires, until a Moroccan army took it in 1591. Its mosques and manuscript libraries survive, and it is now a city in northern Mali.
references: John O. Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: Al-Sadi's Tarikh al-Sudan down to 1613 and other contemporary documents (Brill, 2003)
Elias N. Saad, Social History of Timbuktu: The Role of Muslim Scholars and Notables 1400–1900 (Cambridge University Press, 1983)
John O. Hunwick, The Hidden Treasures of Timbuktu: Historic city of Islamic Africa (Thames and Hudson, 2008)
Michel Abitbol, Tombouctou et les Arma: de la conquête marocaine du Soudan nigérien en 1591 à l'hégémonie de l'empire Peulh du Macina en 1833 (Maisonneuve & Larose, 1979)
Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (Methuen, 1973)
notes: Founding date: the two articles differ. The main article says the town 'became permanent early in the 12th century'; History of Timbuktu says a seasonal settlement of the late 11th or early 12th century became permanent 'either in the 13th or early 14th century'. I gave both under origins and used about 1100 (circa) for 'start' from al-Sadi, as the history article does.

Mansa Musa's annexation: History of Timbuktu says 1324, on his return from pilgrimage; the main article's lead says 'around 1325' for his visit. I used 1324. The Djinguereber Mosque is dated 1327 in the main article and attributed to Mansa Musa in both; I gave the date with the chronicles' attribution.
Moroccan invasion: the main article says the Moroccans invaded in 1590 and occupied Timbuktu in 1591; the history article says 30 May 1591. I used 30 May 1591 and left out 1590.

Leo Africanus's date for the founding (1213 or 1214, by Mansa Sulayman) is given in the main article as his writing, and I attributed it to him. Population figures: about 10,000 by 1300 and about 50,000 in the 1500s (economy section), an estimated medieval peak of 100,000 (history section); no hedge beyond 'estimated'. Shabeni's visit is dated roughly 250 years after Leo's, and the history article says 1780 for his account.

Mungo Park: the history article says 'It is believed that Park was the first Westerner to have reached the city, but he died ... without having the chance to report his findings'. I did not repeat the belief, since Park is not known to have reached it. Robert Adams's claim is doubted by recent scholarship; I said so.

'The 25,000 students' of the three madrasahs, and 'up to 700,000 manuscripts in 2003', are the article's figures; the article also gives different numbers for how many manuscripts were saved in 2013 (90%; 350,000 taken to safety; 300,000 still in Bamako in 2022; and a later claim of fifty thousand in family libraries). I gave the first three. 'Fifteen jihadis' and 'burned 4,202 manuscripts' are quoted from a book excerpt in the article.

2023 blockade: the main article says it 'is classified as ongoing'; I stated it as 8 August 2023 and gave no verdict. I left out the article's account of the current military government. Salt, gold and slaves: the main article adds 'local gold and salt mining', which the history article does not support, so I used the history article's list of trade goods.

Things I wanted but could not find: a date for Sankoré's building more precise than '14th–15th century'; the date of the canal's silting; the article's date for Askia Mohammad I's pilgrimage; anything on Timbuktu in the 19th century beyond the Massina and Toucouleur empires; and the origin of its population figure for 1300.
